periods.jinNorthSouth: Jin and Northern and Southern dynasties
periods.song: Song, Liao, Jin and Western Xia

Xia_dynasty.title: Xia dynasty
Xia_dynasty.text: The first dynasty in traditional histories, said to have been founded by Yu the Great around 2070 BCE; its existence is still debated by scholars.

Erlitou_culture.title: Erlitou culture
Erlitou_culture.text: Palace foundations, bronze ritual vessels and a large city appeared on the middle Yellow River; many scholars see it as an early state and as the Xia culture.

Shang_dynasty.title: Tang overthrows the Xia; the Shang dynasty is founded
Shang_dynasty.text: Tang, leader of the Shang people, defeated Jie of Xia at Mingtiao and founded the Shang dynasty. The Zhengzhou Shang City is a large city site of this period.

Yinxu.title: Pan Geng moves the capital to Yin
Yinxu.text: The Shang king Pan Geng moved the capital to Yin, where it stayed for over two centuries; the Yinxu ruins have yielded palaces, royal tombs and many bronzes.

Oracle_bone_script.title: Oracle bone script
Oracle_bone_script.text: Shang kings inscribed divination records on turtle shells and animal bones, the earliest known systematic Chinese writing and a primary source for Shang history.

Sanxingdui.title: Sanxingdui civilization
Sanxingdui.text: The ancient Shu kingdom left bronze masks with protruding eyes, bronze trees and a gold staff, in a style very different from the Central Plains, showing the multiple origins of Chinese civilization.

Battle_of_Muye.title: Battle of Muye
Battle_of_Muye.text: King Wu of Zhou led an allied army that defeated the forces of King Zhou of Shang; the Shang fell and the Zhou dynasty was founded, with its capital at Haojing.

Gonghe_Regency.title: Revolt of the capital's people and the Gonghe Regency
Gonghe_Regency.text: King Li of Zhou was driven out by the people of the capital and Gong He (or, by another account, the Dukes of Zhou and Shao) ruled in his place. The year 841 BCE marks the beginning of precisely dated Chinese history.

Spring_and_Autumn_period.title: King Ping moves east; the Spring and Autumn period begins
Spring_and_Autumn_period.text: After the Quanrong sacked Haojing, King Ping of Zhou moved the capital to Luoyi. Royal power waned as the feudal lords vied for hegemony, opening the Spring and Autumn period.

Confucius.title: Birth of Confucius
Confucius.text: Confucius founded the Confucian school, taught benevolence and ritual, and ran private schools. Developed by later generations, his ideas dominated East Asian thought for two thousand years.

Partition_of_Jin.title: Partition of Jin
Partition_of_Jin.text: The Han, Zhao and Wei families divided the state of Jin and were recognized as feudal lords by the Zhou king, often seen as the start of the Warring States period.

Shang_Yang.title: Reforms of Shang Yang
Shang_Yang.place: Yueyang, state of Qin (Lintong, Xi'an, Shaanxi)
Shang_Yang.text: Shang Yang rewarded farming and warfare, abolished hereditary privilege and set up counties in Qin, making it the strongest of the Warring States.

Yayoi_period.title: Yayoi period
Yayoi_period.text: Wet-rice farming and metal tools reached Japan from the continent via the Korean Peninsula, bringing settlements and social stratification and replacing the Jōmon culture.

Battle_of_Changping.title: Battle of Changping
Battle_of_Changping.text: The Qin general Bai Qi crushed the Zhao army and reportedly buried hundreds of thousands of surrendered soldiers alive; no single state could resist Qin thereafter.

Qin's_wars_of_unification.title: Qin unifies China
Qin's_wars_of_unification.text: King Ying Zheng of Qin conquered Qi, completing unification. Calling himself the First Emperor, he imposed commanderies and counties and standardized script, weights and measures, and axle widths.

Great_Wall_of_China.title: Building the Great Wall
Great_Wall_of_China.place: Ordos Loop and the northern frontier
Great_Wall_of_China.text: After Meng Tian drove back the Xiongnu, Qin linked and extended the walls of the Warring States, forming the prototype of the Great Wall.

Terracotta_Army.title: Terracotta Army of the First Emperor
Terracotta_Army.text: The First Emperor died and was buried at Mount Li. More than 8,000 life-size clay soldiers guarded his tomb; they were discovered only in 1974.

Dazexiang_uprising.title: Dazexiang uprising
Dazexiang_uprising.text: The conscripts Chen Sheng and Wu Guang rebelled, asking "Are kings, lords and generals born to their rank?"; revolts spread and the Qin dynasty soon collapsed.

Modu_Chanyu.title: Modu Chanyu unites the Xiongnu
Modu_Chanyu.text: Modu killed his father and became chanyu, crushed the Donghu in the east and drove off the Yuezhi in the west, founding the first great nomadic empire of the steppe.

Battle_of_Gaixia.title: Battle of Gaixia; the Han dynasty is founded
Battle_of_Gaixia.text: Liu Bang defeated Xiang Yu, ending the Chu–Han contention and founding the Western Han, later with its capital at Chang'an. The idiom "surrounded by Chu songs" comes from this battle.

Battle_of_Baideng.title: Siege of Baideng
Battle_of_Baideng.text: Emperor Gaozu of Han was besieged by Modu Chanyu for seven days; after escaping, Han turned to marriage alliances and annual tribute to placate the Xiongnu.

Zhang_Qian.title: Zhang Qian's mission to the Western Regions
Zhang_Qian.text: Emperor Wu sent Zhang Qian to ally with the Greater Yuezhi against the Xiongnu. His intelligence on the Western Regions opened the way for the Silk Road.

Battle_of_Mobei.title: Battle of Mobei
Battle_of_Mobei.text: Wei Qing and Huo Qubing struck deep north of the Gobi and shattered the main Xiongnu forces; Huo performed the sacrifice at Mount Langjuxu and the Xiongnu fled far away.

Han_conquest_of_Nanyue.title: Han conquest of Nanyue
Han_conquest_of_Nanyue.text: Han armies destroyed the Nanyue kingdom founded by Zhao Tuo, bringing Lingnan and northern Vietnam under Han commanderies.

Han_conquest_of_Gojoseon.title: Han conquest of Wiman Joseon
Han_conquest_of_Gojoseon.text: Emperor Wu of Han conquered Wiman Joseon and set up four commanderies, including Lelang, in the northern Korean Peninsula.

Records_of_the_Grand_Historian.title: Records of the Grand Historian completed
Records_of_the_Grand_Historian.text: Sima Qian completed the Shiji, a biographical-style general history covering some 2,500 years from the Yellow Emperor to Emperor Wu, the model for later official histories.

Xin_dynasty.title: Wang Mang usurps the Han
Xin_dynasty.text: The consort kinsman Wang Mang replaced the Han and founded the Xin dynasty with archaizing reforms. Their failure sparked the Lülin and Red Eyebrows rebellions.

Emperor_Guangwu_of_Han.title: Restoration under Emperor Guangwu; the Eastern Han
Emperor_Guangwu_of_Han.text: Liu Xiu re-established the Han dynasty with its capital at Luoyang, known as the Eastern Han.

King_of_Na_gold_seal.title: King of Na gold seal
King_of_Na_gold_seal.text: Emperor Guangwu granted a gold seal to an envoy from the Na state of Wa. Found on Shikanoshima, Fukuoka, in 1784, it is early physical evidence of China–Japan contacts.

White_Horse_Temple.title: Founding of the White Horse Temple
White_Horse_Temple.text: Emperor Ming of Han is said to have sent envoys who brought back monks and sutras, and the White Horse Temple in Luoyang is regarded as China's first Buddhist temple.

Cai_Lun.title: Cai Lun improves papermaking
Cai_Lun.text: The eunuch Cai Lun made light, cheap paper from bark, hemp, rags and the like; paper gradually replaced bamboo slips and silk.

Yellow_Turban_Rebellion.title: Yellow Turban Rebellion
Yellow_Turban_Rebellion.text: Zhang Jue organized hundreds of thousands of peasants through the Way of Great Peace. The revolt was crushed, but local magnates and warlords grew powerful.

Battle_of_Red_Cliffs.title: Battle of Red Cliffs
Battle_of_Red_Cliffs.text: The allied forces of Sun Quan and Liu Bei routed Cao Cao's southward advance with fire, setting up the tripartite division of the Three Kingdoms.

Three_Kingdoms.title: Cao Pi replaces the Han; the Three Kingdoms
Three_Kingdoms.text: Cao Pi forced Emperor Xian of Han to abdicate and founded Wei. Liu Bei then proclaimed himself emperor in Chengdu and Sun Quan in Wuchang.

Conquest_of_Wu_by_Jin.title: Western Jin conquers Wu and reunifies China
Conquest_of_Wu_by_Jin.text: Jin forces sailed down the Yangtze and the Wu ruler Sun Hao surrendered, ending the Three Kingdoms period.

Disaster_of_Yongjia.title: Disaster of Yongjia
Disaster_of_Yongjia.text: The Xiongnu-founded Han Zhao took Luoyang and captured Emperor Huai of Jin. The north fell into the wars of the Sixteen Kingdoms and masses of people fled south.

Mogao_Caves.title: Mogao Caves begun
Mogao_Caves.text: The monk Yuezun carved the first cave at Mingsha Mountain. Over the next thousand years more than 700 caves were cut, preserving a wealth of murals and manuscripts.

Battle_of_Fei_River.title: Battle of Fei River
Battle_of_Fei_River.text: The outnumbered Eastern Jin defeated the vast Former Qin army, which fled at "the whistle of the wind and the cry of cranes". Former Qin soon collapsed and the north–south division continued.

Gwanggaeto_Stele.title: Gwanggaeto Stele
Gwanggaeto_Stele.text: King Jangsu of Goguryeo erected a stele recording the deeds of his father King Gwanggaeto, a key source for Goguryeo and early Northeast Asian history.

Emperor_Xiaowen_of_Northern_Wei.title: Emperor Xiaowen moves the Northern Wei capital to Luoyang
Emperor_Xiaowen_of_Northern_Wei.text: Emperor Xiaowen moved the capital from Pingcheng to Luoyang, pursued sinicization reforms that replaced Xianbei surnames with Chinese ones, and began the Longmen Grottoes.

Buddhism_in_Japan.title: Buddhism reaches Japan
Buddhism_in_Japan.text: King Seong of Baekje sent Buddhist images and scriptures to Wa. The Soga and Mononobe clans clashed over them, and the pro-Buddhist faction prevailed.

Sui_conquest_of_Chen.title: Sui conquers Chen and reunifies north and south
Sui_conquest_of_Chen.text: Sui troops crossed the Yangtze and took Jiankang, ending nearly three centuries of division since the late Western Jin.

Grand_Canal_(China).title: Building the Grand Canal
Grand_Canal_(China).place: Tongji Canal (Luoyang to the Huai River)
Grand_Canal_(China).text: Emperor Yang of Sui mobilized a million laborers to dig canals linking the Yellow, Huai and Yangtze rivers, which became the lifeline carrying southern grain north.

Imperial_examination.title: Imperial examinations established
Imperial_examination.text: The Sui created the jinshi degree to select officials by examination. The system lasted until 1905 and was copied in Korea and Vietnam.

Battle_of_Salsu.title: Battle of Salsu
Battle_of_Salsu.text: During Emperor Yang's invasion of Goguryeo, Eulji Mundeok routed the Sui army at the Salsu River. Repeated campaigns exhausted Sui, which soon fell.

Tang_dynasty.title: Founding of the Tang dynasty
Tang_dynasty.text: Li Yuan proclaimed himself emperor in Chang'an and founded the Tang. Tang Chang'an was one of the largest cities in the world at the time.

Princess_Wencheng.title: Princess Wencheng goes to Tibet
Princess_Wencheng.text: Emperor Taizong of Tang married Princess Wencheng to the Tibetan emperor Songtsen Gampo; the artisans and Buddhist images that accompanied her fostered Han–Tibetan exchange.

Taika_Reform.title: Taika Reform
Taika_Reform.text: Prince Naka no Ōe and Nakatomi no Kamatari destroyed the Soga clan and introduced Tang-style reforms of public land and the ritsuryō legal system.

Xuanzang.title: Xuanzang returns from India
Xuanzang.text: After a 17-year pilgrimage to India, Xuanzang brought back more than 600 texts and dictated the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions.

Battle_of_Baekgang.title: Battle of Baekgang
Battle_of_Baekgang.place: Mouth of the Baek River (Geum River, South Korea)
Battle_of_Baekgang.text: A Tang–Silla fleet crushed the navies of Wa and the Baekje restoration forces; the Baekje restoration failed and Wa withdrew from the Korean Peninsula.

Unified_Silla.title: Silla unifies the Korean Peninsula
Unified_Silla.text: Having destroyed Baekje and Goguryeo in alliance with Tang, Silla then drove the Tang army north of the Taedong River and unified most of the peninsula.

Balhae.title: Founding of Balhae
Balhae.text: Dae Joyeong founded a state with the Sumo Mohe and Goguryeo refugees; later invested by the Tang, it was called the "flourishing land east of the sea".

Heijō-kyō.title: Capital moved to Heijō-kyō
Heijō-kyō.text: Japan built Heijō-kyō on the model of Tang Chang'an, beginning the Nara period.

An_Lushan_Rebellion.title: An Lushan Rebellion
An_Lushan_Rebellion.text: The military governor An Lushan rebelled and took Luoyang and Chang'an. After eight years of war the Tang went into decline, with regional warlords entrenched.

Heian-kyō.title: Capital moved to Heian-kyō
Heian-kyō.text: Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyō; Kyoto remained Japan's imperial capital for over a thousand years, and the Heian period began.

Khmer_Empire.title: Founding of the Angkorian Khmer Empire
Khmer_Empire.text: Jayavarman II declared independence and proclaimed himself universal monarch; the Khmer Empire dominated mainland Southeast Asia for centuries.

Uyghur_Khaganate.title: Fall of the Uyghur Khaganate
Uyghur_Khaganate.text: The Kyrgyz sacked the Uyghur capital; the Uyghurs moved west to Gaochang and the Hexi Corridor and became among the ancestors of today's Uyghurs.

Diamond_Sutra.title: Printed Diamond Sutra
Diamond_Sutra.text: The Diamond Sutra printed in 868 is the earliest surviving dated woodblock-printed book; it was found in the Mogao Caves in 1900.

Huang_Chao.title: Huang Chao Rebellion
Huang_Chao.text: The salt smuggler Huang Chao rebelled, fought across China and took Chang'an, proclaiming himself emperor. The Tang suppressed the revolt but survived in name only.

Five_Dynasties_and_Ten_Kingdoms_period.title: Fall of the Tang; Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms
Five_Dynasties_and_Ten_Kingdoms_period.text: Zhu Wen usurped the Tang and founded the Later Liang. For half a century five dynasties succeeded one another in the north while over ten kingdoms coexisted in the south.

Goryeo.title: Founding of Goryeo
Goryeo.text: Wang Geon founded Goryeo and later unified the Later Three Kingdoms. The English name "Korea" derives from Goryeo.

Battle_of_Bạch_Đằng_(938).title: Battle of Bạch Đằng (938)
Battle_of_Bạch_Đằng_(938).text: Ngô Quyền routed the Southern Han fleet with a field of stakes, ending about a thousand years of Chinese rule over northern Vietnam and opening the way to independence.

Song_dynasty.title: Chenqiao mutiny; the Northern Song is founded
Song_dynasty.text: Zhao Kuangyin was draped in the imperial yellow robe and founded the Song, which favored civil rule and stripped generals of their commands "over a cup of wine".

Chanyuan_Treaty.title: Treaty of Chanyuan
Chanyuan_Treaty.text: Song and Liao made peace, with Song paying Liao annual tribute. The two states then kept the peace for over a century.

Lý_dynasty.title: Lý dynasty moves the capital to Thăng Long
Lý_dynasty.text: Lý Thái Tổ (Lý Công Uẩn) moved the capital to Đại La and renamed it Thăng Long; Hanoi has been Vietnam's political center ever since.

Western_Xia.title: Founding of the Western Xia
Western_Xia.text: The Tangut leader Li Yuanhao proclaimed himself emperor of Great Xia and created the Tangut script.

Movable_type.title: Bi Sheng invents movable type
Movable_type.text: According to Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays, the commoner Bi Sheng printed with movable type made of baked clay, some 400 years before Europe.

Pagan_Kingdom.title: Anawrahta takes the throne; Pagan rises
Pagan_Kingdom.text: After taking the throne, Anawrahta unified the Irrawaddy valley, promoted Theravada Buddhism and built thousands of pagodas.

Wang_Anshi.title: Reforms of Wang Anshi
Wang_Anshi.text: Emperor Shenzong appointed Wang Anshi to enact the Green Sprouts, hired-service and other New Policies to enrich the state, fueling bitter factional strife.

Zizhi_Tongjian.title: Zizhi Tongjian completed
Zizhi_Tongjian.text: Over 19 years Sima Guang compiled a chronological general history covering 1,362 years from the Warring States to the Five Dynasties.

Jin_dynasty_(1115–1234).title: Founding of the Jin dynasty
Jin_dynasty_(1115–1234).text: The Jurchen leader Wanyan Aguda proclaimed the Jin. Ten years later Jin destroyed the Liao, and in 1127 it overthrew the Northern Song.

Jingkang_incident.title: Jingkang incident
Jingkang_incident.text: Jin troops took Kaifeng and carried off emperors Huizong and Qinzong with the imperial clan, ending the Northern Song. Emperor Gaozong re-established the Song in the south as the Southern Song.

Yue_Fei.title: Execution of Yue Fei; Treaty of Shaoxing
Yue_Fei.text: The anti-Jin general Yue Fei was put to death on a charge of "perhaps" (mo xu you). Song and Jin made peace, with the Huai River and Dasan Pass as the border.

Battle_of_Dan-no-ura.title: Battle of Dan-no-ura
Battle_of_Dan-no-ura.text: The Minamoto destroyed the Taira in a naval battle; Minamoto no Yoritomo then set up a shogunate at Kamakura, beginning the era of warrior rule in Japan.

Genghis_Khan.title: Genghis Khan unites the Mongols
Genghis_Khan.place: Source of the Onon River (Khentii, Mongolia)
Genghis_Khan.text: Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan at a kurultai and founded the Great Mongol State, which went on to conquer most of Eurasia.

Battle_of_Zhongdu.title: Mongols take the Jin capital Zhongdu
Battle_of_Zhongdu.text: After Emperor Xuanzong of Jin moved south to Kaifeng, the Mongols besieged and captured the Jin capital Zhongdu.

Siege_of_Caizhou.title: Siege of Caizhou; fall of the Jin
Siege_of_Caizhou.text: Allied Mongol and Southern Song forces stormed Caizhou; Emperor Aizong of Jin killed himself and the Jin dynasty ended. War between Song and the Mongols soon followed.

Sukhothai_Kingdom.title: Founding of the Sukhothai Kingdom
Sukhothai_Kingdom.text: The Tai threw off Khmer rule and founded Sukhothai; tradition holds that the Thai script was created under King Ram Khamhaeng.

Yuan_dynasty.title: Kublai Khan founds the Yuan dynasty
Yuan_dynasty.text: Kublai took the dynastic name Yuan from the Book of Changes phrase "great is the primal Qian", and the next year made Dadu his capital.

Mongol_invasions_of_Japan.title: Mongol invasions of Japan
Mongol_invasions_of_Japan.text: Yuan and Goryeo forces twice crossed the sea to attack Japan (1274, 1281), failing because of Japanese defenses and storms. The Japanese called the storms "kamikaze".

Marco_Polo.title: Marco Polo reaches Shangdu
Marco_Polo.text: The Venetian merchant Marco Polo met Kublai Khan. His travel account fired European imaginations about China.

Battle_of_Yamen.title: Battle of Yamen; fall of the Southern Song
Battle_of_Yamen.text: The Yuan navy destroyed the last Southern Song fleet; Lu Xiufu leapt into the sea carrying the boy emperor Zhao Bing, and the Southern Song ended.

Battle_of_Bạch_Đằng_(1288).title: Battle of Bạch Đằng (1288)
Battle_of_Bạch_Đằng_(1288).text: Trần Hưng Đạo used Ngô Quyền's stake tactic to repel the third Yuan invasion, preserving Đại Việt's independence.

Red_Turban_Rebellions.title: Red Turban Rebellions
Red_Turban_Rebellions.text: Liu Futong and others organized an uprising through the White Lotus sect; wearing red head cloths, the anti-Yuan revolts quickly spread across the country.

Ayutthaya_Kingdom.title: Founding of the Ayutthaya Kingdom
Ayutthaya_Kingdom.text: King U Thong founded Ayutthaya, which later absorbed Sukhothai and remained the leading power of Siam for over four centuries.

Battle_of_Lake_Poyang.title: Battle of Lake Poyang
Battle_of_Lake_Poyang.text: Zhu Yuanzhang used fire attacks to defeat Chen Youliang's fleet of giant ships, one of the largest naval battles of the medieval world.

Ming_dynasty.title: Founding of the Ming dynasty
Ming_dynasty.text: Zhu Yuanzhang proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Ming. That year Ming troops entered Dadu and the last Yuan emperor fled north of the Gobi.

Joseon.title: Founding of Joseon
Joseon.place: Gaegyeong; capital moved to Hanyang (Seoul) in 1394
Joseon.text: Yi Seong-gye overthrew Goryeo and founded the Joseon dynasty, which championed Confucianism, lasted over 500 years and was renamed the Korean Empire in 1897.

Ming_treasure_voyages.title: Zheng He's treasure voyages
Ming_treasure_voyages.text: Zheng He led fleets of more than 200 ships on seven voyages, reaching as far as the East African coast. The voyages ceased after the Xuande reign.

Forbidden_City.title: Yongle Emperor moves the capital to Beijing
Forbidden_City.text: With the Forbidden City completed, the Ming formally moved its capital to Beijing, which remained the capital of the Ming and Qing for nearly 500 years.

Later_Lê_dynasty.title: Lê Lợi founds the Later Lê dynasty
Later_Lê_dynasty.text: Lê Lợi led the Lam Sơn uprising that expelled the Ming army and founded the Later Lê dynasty, restoring Vietnamese independence.

Ryukyu_Kingdom.title: Unification of the Ryukyu Kingdom
Ryukyu_Kingdom.text: Shō Hashi unified Hokuzan, Chūzan and Nanzan; through tributary trade with the Ming, Ryukyu became an entrepôt of East Asian seas.

Hunminjeongeum.title: Promulgation of Hunminjeongeum
Hunminjeongeum.text: King Sejong the Great of Joseon promulgated the phonetic script Hunminjeongeum, today's Korean alphabet (Hangul).

Tumu_Crisis.title: Tumu Crisis
Tumu_Crisis.text: The Zhengtong Emperor was defeated and captured while personally campaigning against the Oirats; Yu Qian enthroned the Jingtai Emperor and organized the defense of Beijing.

Ōnin_War.title: Ōnin War
Ōnin_War.text: A shogunal succession dispute became an eleven-year civil war that left Kyoto in ashes and ushered Japan into the Sengoku period.

Portuguese_Macau.title: Portuguese settle in Macau
Portuguese_Macau.text: The Portuguese were permitted to live and trade in Macau, which became a key base for European trade and missions in East Asia.

Matteo_Ricci.title: Matteo Ricci arrives in China
Matteo_Ricci.text: The Jesuit Matteo Ricci settled in Zhaoqing and later reached Beijing. He and Xu Guangqi translated Euclid's Elements, furthering Sino-Western learning.

Japanese_invasions_of_Korea_(1592–1598).title: Imjin War (Japanese invasions of Korea)
Japanese_invasions_of_Korea_(1592–1598).text: Toyotomi Hideyoshi invaded Korea; the Ming sent troops to aid Joseon, and Yi Sun-sin's navy repeatedly defeated the Japanese. Japan withdrew in 1598.

Battle_of_Sekigahara.title: Battle of Sekigahara
Battle_of_Sekigahara.text: Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated the Western Army and three years later opened a shogunate in Edo, beginning more than two centuries of the Edo period.

Later_Jin_(1616–1636).title: Nurhaci founds the Later Jin
Later_Jin_(1616–1636).text: Nurhaci united the Jurchen tribes and founded the Later Jin; in 1636 Hong Taiji renamed the state Qing.

Battle_of_Sarhū.title: Battle of Sarhū
Battle_of_Sarhū.text: The Later Jin concentrated its forces to defeat the four Ming columns one by one, reversing the balance between Ming and Qing in Liaodong.

Dutch_Formosa.title: The Dutch occupy Taiwan
Dutch_Formosa.text: The Dutch East India Company built Fort Zeelandia in southern Taiwan and established colonial rule.

Battle_of_Shanhai_Pass.title: Battle of Shanhai Pass; the Qing enter China proper
Battle_of_Shanhai_Pass.text: Li Zicheng took Beijing and the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself. Wu Sangui let the Qing through the pass; they defeated Li and made Beijing their capital.

Potala_Palace.title: Rebuilding of the Potala Palace
Potala_Palace.text: After establishing the Ganden Phodrang government, the 5th Dalai Lama rebuilt the Potala Palace on the Red Hill as the religious and political center.

Siege_of_Fort_Zeelandia.title: Koxinga takes Taiwan
Siege_of_Fort_Zeelandia.text: Koxinga (Zheng Chenggong) besieged Fort Zeelandia for nine months until the Dutch surrendered and left Taiwan.

Battle_of_Penghu.title: Battle of Penghu; Qing annexes Taiwan
Battle_of_Penghu.text: Shi Lang's Qing fleet defeated the Zheng navy and Zheng Keshuang surrendered; the next year the Qing set up a prefecture in Taiwan.

Treaty_of_Nerchinsk.title: Treaty of Nerchinsk
Treaty_of_Nerchinsk.text: After the siege of Albazin, Qing and Russia set the border along the Argun River and the Stanovoy Range, China's first boundary treaty with a European state.

Treaty_of_Kyakhta_(1727).title: Treaty of Kyakhta
Treaty_of_Kyakhta_(1727).text: Qing and Russia delimited the border along Khalkha Mongolia and made Kyakhta the trading post between the two empires.

Dzungar–Qing_Wars.title: Qing destroys the Dzungars
Dzungar–Qing_Wars.text: Qing armies crushed Amursana's revolt; war and smallpox nearly wiped out the Dzungars, and two years later all the lands north and south of the Tian Shan came under Qing rule.

Canton_System.title: Canton System
Canton_System.text: The Qianlong Emperor restricted Western ships to trading at Guangzhou, where the Thirteen Hongs monopolized foreign trade until the Opium War.

Siku_Quanshu.title: Compilation of the Siku Quanshu
Siku_Quanshu.text: The Qianlong Emperor ordered China's largest collectanea, with over 3,000 titles; at the same time many books were banned and destroyed.

Macartney_Embassy.title: Macartney Embassy
Macartney_Embassy.text: The British embassy's request to expand trade was rejected by the Qianlong Emperor, and the two sides also clashed over court ritual.

Nguyễn_dynasty.title: Founding of the Nguyễn dynasty
Nguyễn_dynasty.text: Nguyễn Phúc Ánh unified Vietnam, made Huế his capital and founded Vietnam's last dynasty.

First_Opium_War.title: First Opium War
First_Opium_War.text: After Lin Zexu destroyed opium at Humen, Britain sent an expeditionary force. The Qing defeat marks the start of China's modern history.

Treaty_of_Nanking.title: Treaty of Nanking
Treaty_of_Nanking.text: The Qing ceded Hong Kong Island, opened Guangzhou, Xiamen, Fuzhou, Ningbo and Shanghai to trade, and paid an indemnity of 21 million silver dollars.

Taiping_Rebellion.title: Taiping Rebellion
Taiping_Rebellion.text: Hong Xiuquan launched a rebellion and later made Tianjing (Nanjing) his capital. More than a decade of civil war killed tens of millions.

Perry_Expedition.title: Arrival of the Black Ships
Perry_Expedition.text: US Commodore Matthew Perry arrived with a squadron demanding entry; the next year Japan signed a treaty ending over two centuries of seclusion.

Treaty_of_Aigun.title: Treaty of Aigun
Treaty_of_Aigun.text: Russia forced the Qing to cede more than 600,000 km² of land north of the Amur River.

Convention_of_Peking.title: Burning of the Old Summer Palace and the Convention of Peking
Convention_of_Peking.text: Anglo-French forces entered Beijing and burned the Old Summer Palace. The Qing ceded Kowloon, and in a following treaty with Russia ceded the lands east of the Ussuri River.

Self-Strengthening_Movement.title: Self-Strengthening Movement
Self-Strengthening_Movement.text: Zeng Guofan founded the Anqing Arsenal; Li Hongzhang and others went on to build the Jiangnan Arsenal, the Fuzhou Navy Yard and the Beiyang Fleet.

Meiji_Restoration.title: Meiji Restoration
Meiji_Restoration.text: Imperial rule was restored and the shogunate ended. Japan pursued sweeping Westernizing reforms and quickly turned to industrialization and overseas expansion.

Japan–Korea_Treaty_of_1876.title: Treaty of Ganghwa
Japan–Korea_Treaty_of_1876.text: Through gunboat diplomacy Japan forced Joseon to open its ports and rejected Qing suzerainty over Korea.

Ryukyu_Disposition.title: Ryukyu Disposition
Ryukyu_Disposition.text: Japan abolished the Ryukyu Kingdom and created Okinawa Prefecture. The Qing protested but could not change the outcome.

Sino-French_War.title: Sino-French War
Sino-French_War.text: China and France went to war over Vietnam. Qing forces won at Zhennan Pass, but the Qing ultimately recognized the French protectorate over Vietnam.

First_Sino-Japanese_War.title: First Sino-Japanese War
First_Sino-Japanese_War.text: Japan and the Qing fought over Korea, and the Beiyang Fleet was destroyed at the Battle of the Yalu River and the Battle of Weihaiwei.

Treaty_of_Shimonoseki.title: Treaty of Shimonoseki
Treaty_of_Shimonoseki.text: The Qing recognized Korea's "independence", ceded Taiwan and Penghu, and paid an indemnity of 200 million taels of silver.

Hundred_Days'_Reform.title: Hundred Days' Reform
Hundred_Days'_Reform.text: The Guangxu Emperor enlisted Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao to carry out reforms, overturned after only 103 days by a coup led by Empress Dowager Cixi.

Boxer_Rebellion.title: Boxer Rebellion and the Eight-Nation Alliance
Boxer_Rebellion.text: The Boxers besieged the Legation Quarter and the Eight-Nation Alliance captured Beijing. The next year the Qing signed the Boxer Protocol, paying an indemnity of 450 million taels.

Russo-Japanese_War.title: Russo-Japanese War
Russo-Japanese_War.text: Japan and Russia fought in Northeast China. Victorious Japan took over Russia's interests in southern Manchuria, the first Asian nation to defeat a European power.

Japan–Korea_Treaty_of_1910.title: Japan annexes Korea
Japan–Korea_Treaty_of_1910.text: With the Japan–Korea Annexation Treaty the Korean Empire ended, and the peninsula became a Japanese colony until 1945.

Wuchang_uprising.title: Wuchang Uprising; the 1911 Revolution
Wuchang_uprising.text: New Army troops rose up and seized Wuchang, and province after province declared independence. The emperor abdicated the next year, ending over two thousand years of imperial rule.

Republic_of_China_(1912–1949).title: Founding of the Republic of China
Republic_of_China_(1912–1949).text: Sun Yat-sen took office as provisional president in Nanjing and the Provisional Government of the Republic of China was established, ending more than two thousand years of imperial rule.

March_1st_Movement.title: March 1st Movement
March_1st_Movement.text: Koreans proclaimed a declaration of independence and held mass peaceful demonstrations, which the Japanese colonial authorities suppressed.

May_Fourth_Movement.title: May Fourth Movement
May_Fourth_Movement.text: Students protested the Paris Peace Conference's transfer of German rights in Shandong to Japan. The movement spurred the New Culture Movement and the spread of vernacular Chinese.

Mongolian_Revolution_of_1921.title: Mongolian Revolution of 1921
Mongolian_Revolution_of_1921.text: The Mongolian People's Party took power with the backing of the Soviet Red Army, and the Mongolian People's Republic was proclaimed in 1924.

1st_National_Congress_of_the_Chinese_Com.title: Founding of the Chinese Communist Party
1st_National_Congress_of_the_Chinese_Com.text: The First National Congress of the CCP opened in Shanghai and closed on a boat on South Lake in Jiaxing.

1923_Great_Kantō_earthquake.title: Great Kantō earthquake
1923_Great_Kantō_earthquake.text: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake and the fires it caused killed about 100,000 people, and was followed by a massacre of Koreans.

Northern_Expedition.title: Northern Expedition
Northern_Expedition.text: The National Revolutionary Army set out from Guangzhou, defeated the Beiyang warlords and in 1928 nominally unified the country with its capital at Nanjing.

1931_China_floods.title: 1931 China floods
1931_China_floods.text: The Yangtze, the Huai and the Grand Canal flooded at once, leaving Wuhan underwater for months; it was one of the deadliest natural disasters of the 20th century.

Mukden_Incident.title: Mukden Incident
Mukden_Incident.text: Japan's Kwantung Army set off an explosion on the South Manchuria Railway near Liutiaohu, blamed Chinese troops, then occupied the Northeast and set up Manchukuo the next year.

Long_March.title: Long March
Long_March.text: The Central Red Army abandoned the Central Soviet Area and marched some 25,000 li, reaching northern Shaanxi in October 1935.

Marco_Polo_Bridge_incident.title: Marco Polo Bridge Incident
Marco_Polo_Bridge_incident.text: Japanese troops provoked a clash at the Marco Polo Bridge, and China began full-scale resistance against Japan.

Nanjing_Massacre.title: Nanjing Massacre
Nanjing_Massacre.text: After capturing Nanjing, Japanese troops massacred civilians and prisoners of war on a vast scale over six weeks and committed widespread rape, looting and arson.

Battle_of_Taierzhuang.title: Battle of Taierzhuang
Battle_of_Taierzhuang.text: Chinese forces under Li Zongren inflicted heavy losses on the Japanese, the first major victory on the main front since full-scale war began.

Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasak.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasak.text: The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki; between 150,000 and over 200,000 people in the two cities died that year.

Surrender_of_Japan.title: Surrender of Japan
Surrender_of_Japan.text: Emperor Hirohito announced by radio the acceptance of the Potsdam Declaration. Japan signed the instrument of surrender on 2 September, ending World War II and Japanese rule over Taiwan and Korea.

Huaihai_campaign.title: Huaihai Campaign
Huaihai_campaign.text: One of the largest campaigns of the Chinese Civil War. The PLA destroyed more than 500,000 Nationalist troops, settling control north of the Yangtze.

Proclamation_of_the_People's_Republic_of.title: Founding of the People's Republic of China
Proclamation_of_the_People's_Republic_of.text: From the Tiananmen rostrum, Mao Zedong proclaimed the founding of the Central People's Government of the People's Republic of China.

Retreat_of_the_government_of_the_Republi.title: ROC government retreats to Taiwan
Retreat_of_the_government_of_the_Republi.text: After losing the Civil War, the government of the Republic of China moved to Taipei, beginning the separate rule of the two sides of the Taiwan Strait.

Korean_War.title: Korean War
Korean_War.text: North Korean troops crossed the 38th parallel. The US-led UN forces and the Chinese People's Volunteers entered the war in turn; an armistice was signed in 1953.

Korean_Armistice_Agreement.title: Korean Armistice Agreement
Korean_Armistice_Agreement.text: The belligerents signed an armistice at Panmunjom, setting a military demarcation line and demilitarized zone; no peace treaty has been signed to this day.

Battle_of_Dien_Bien_Phu.title: Battle of Điện Biên Phủ
Battle_of_Dien_Bien_Phu.text: Viet Minh forces besieged the French stronghold for over fifty days and won. The Geneva Conference then temporarily divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel.

Great_Chinese_Famine.title: Great Chinese Famine
Great_Chinese_Famine.place: Nationwide (worst in Xinyang, Henan and elsewhere)
Great_Chinese_Famine.text: Inflated claims and excessive grain procurement during the Great Leap Forward, compounded by natural disasters, caused the 1959–1961 famine, with deaths estimated in the tens of millions.

Shinkansen.title: Tōkaidō Shinkansen opens
Shinkansen.text: The world's first high-speed railway opened just before the Tokyo Olympics, a symbol of Japan's rapid postwar economic growth.

596_(nuclear_test).title: China's first atomic bomb test
596_(nuclear_test).text: China conducted its first successful nuclear test at Lop Nur, becoming the fifth nuclear-armed state.

Cultural_Revolution.title: Cultural Revolution
Cultural_Revolution.text: Launched by Mao Zedong, the decade-long political movement brought mass persecution, social upheaval and cultural destruction, ending in 1976.

1972_visit_by_Richard_Nixon_to_China.title: Nixon's visit to China
1972_visit_by_Richard_Nixon_to_China.text: US President Richard Nixon visited China and issued the Shanghai Communiqué, beginning the normalization of China–US relations.

1976_Tangshan_earthquake.title: Tangshan earthquake
1976_Tangshan_earthquake.text: A magnitude 7.8 earthquake almost entirely destroyed the city; the official death toll exceeded 240,000.

Chinese_economic_reform.title: Reform and opening up
Chinese_economic_reform.text: The Third Plenum of the 11th CCP Central Committee shifted the focus to economic development, followed by the household responsibility system and opening to the outside world.

Sino-Vietnamese_War.title: Sino-Vietnamese War
Sino-Vietnamese_War.text: Chinese troops attacked Vietnam's northern border areas and withdrew a month later; border clashes continued until the late 1980s.

Shenzhen.title: Shenzhen Special Economic Zone established
Shenzhen.text: Starting as a small border town, Shenzhen became the testing ground of China's reforms and within decades a metropolis of over ten million.

June_Democratic_Struggle.title: June Democratic Struggle
June_Democratic_Struggle.text: Nationwide protests forced the military government to accept direct presidential elections, starting South Korea's democratization.

1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massa.title: Tiananmen Square protests and massacre
1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massa.text: Crowds led by students gathered in Tiananmen Square calling for political reform. On the night of 3–4 June the army cleared the square, killing and wounding many civilians.

1990_Mongolian_democratic_revolution.title: Mongolian Democratic Revolution
1990_Mongolian_democratic_revolution.text: Peaceful demonstrations led the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party to give up one-party rule; Mongolia held multiparty elections and moved to a market economy.

1996_Taiwanese_presidential_election.title: Taiwan's first direct presidential election
1996_Taiwanese_presidential_election.text: Taiwan held its first direct election of its leader, amid heightened tension in the Taiwan Strait in the run-up to the vote.

Transfer_of_sovereignty_over_Hong_Kong.title: Handover of Hong Kong
Transfer_of_sovereignty_over_Hong_Kong.text: Britain transferred sovereignty over Hong Kong to the People's Republic of China, which set up the Hong Kong SAR under "one country, two systems".

Transfer_of_sovereignty_over_Macau.title: Handover of Macau
Transfer_of_sovereignty_over_Macau.text: Portugal transferred sovereignty over Macau to China, ending more than four centuries of Portuguese administration.

Three_Gorges_Dam.title: Three Gorges Dam begins filling
Three_Gorges_Dam.text: The world's largest hydropower station began filling its reservoir; more than a million residents were relocated.

2008_Sichuan_earthquake.title: Wenchuan earthquake
2008_Sichuan_earthquake.text: A magnitude 8.0 earthquake killed nearly 70,000 people and left about 18,000 missing.

2008_Summer_Olympics.title: Beijing Olympics
2008_Summer_Olympics.text: The 29th Summer Olympic Games opened in Beijing, the first Olympics hosted by China.

Dong_Zhuo.title: Dong Zhuo enters Luoyang
Dong_Zhuo.text: After the eunuchs and the consort clan destroyed each other, the Liang warlord Dong Zhuo led his troops into Luoyang, deposed the Young Emperor, enthroned Emperor Xian and seized control of the court; the great turmoil began here.

Campaign_against_Dong_Zhuo.title: Guandong coalition against Dong Zhuo
Campaign_against_Dong_Zhuo.text: Yuan Shao, Cao Cao and other lords east of the passes rose against Dong Zhuo. Dong burned Luoyang and moved Emperor Xian west to Chang'an; the coalition then broke up and warlords carved up the land.

Battle_of_Guandu.title: Battle of Guandu
Battle_of_Guandu.text: Cao Cao raided Wuchao and burned Yuan Shao's grain, defeating a larger army; he then gradually unified the north.

Longzhong_Plan.title: Longzhong Plan
Longzhong_Plan.text: After Liu Bei visited his cottage three times, Zhuge Liang proposed allying with Wu against Cao and holding both Jing and Yi; this roughly became the threefold division of the realm.

Battle_of_Mount_Dingjun.title: Battle of Mount Dingjun
Battle_of_Mount_Dingjun.text: Huang Zhong killed Cao's general Xiahou Yuan; Liu Bei took Hanzhong and styled himself King of Hanzhong.

Battle_of_Fancheng.title: Battle of Fancheng and Lü Meng's seizure of Jing
Battle_of_Fancheng.text: Guan Yu attacked Fancheng and drowned seven armies in a flood, shaking the realm; Sun Quan sent Lü Meng to take Jing Province by surprise, and Guan Yu was defeated and killed.

Shu_Han.title: Liu Bei becomes emperor; Shu Han founded
Shu_Han.text: The year after Cao Pi ended the Han, Liu Bei, a member of the Han imperial clan, became emperor at Chengdu with the dynastic name Han, known to history as Shu Han.

Battle_of_Xiaoting.title: Battle of Yiling
Battle_of_Xiaoting.text: Liu Bei attacked Wu to regain Jing Province but was crushed when Lu Xun burned his line of camps; he died the next year at Baidicheng.

Zhuge_Liang's_Southern_Campaign.title: Zhuge Liang's southern campaign
Zhuge_Liang's_Southern_Campaign.text: Zhuge Liang put down a revolt of local strongmen in Nanzhong; tradition says he captured Meng Huo seven times, winning hearts rather than battles and securing Shu Han's rear.

Zhuge_Liang's_Northern_Expeditions.title: Zhuge Liang's northern expedition; Jieting lost
Zhuge_Liang's_Northern_Expeditions.text: On Zhuge Liang's first northern expedition, Ma Su disobeyed orders and was beaten at Jieting by the Wei general Zhang He; the campaign failed and Zhuge Liang tearfully had Ma Su executed.

Eastern_Wu.title: Sun Quan becomes emperor
Eastern_Wu.text: Sun Quan became emperor at Wuchang with the dynastic name Wu and moved his capital to Jianye the same year; all three kingdoms now had emperors.

Battle_of_Wuzhang_Plains.title: Battle of Wuzhang Plains
Battle_of_Wuzhang_Plains.text: On his fifth northern expedition Zhuge Liang faced Sima Yi for more than a hundred days and died in camp; the Shu army withdrew.

Incident_at_the_Gaoping_Tombs.title: Incident at the Gaoping Tombs
Incident_at_the_Gaoping_Tombs.text: While Cao Shuang escorted the Wei emperor out of the city to the imperial tombs, Sima Yi staged a coup and destroyed him; power in Cao Wei passed to the Sima clan.

Conquest_of_Shu_by_Wei.title: Wei conquers Shu Han
Conquest_of_Shu_by_Wei.text: Deng Ai slipped through Yinping and reached Chengdu; the Later Ruler Liu Shan surrendered and Shu Han fell.

Jin_dynasty_(266–420).title: Sima Yan founds the Jin dynasty
Jin_dynasty_(266–420).text: Sima Yan forced the last Wei emperor to abdicate and founded the Jin dynasty, known as the Western Jin.

War_of_the_Eight_Princes.title: War of the Eight Princes: Sima Lun deposes and kills Empress Jia
War_of_the_Eight_Princes.text: Sima Lun, Prince of Zhao, deposed and killed Empress Jia, and the princes rose one after another to fight for the court. The civil war lasted until 306, crippling the Western Jin and letting leaders of various peoples rise.

Cheng_Han.title: Li Xiong founds Cheng Han
Cheng_Han.text: Li Xiong, leader of the Cong people, declared himself king at Chengdu and emperor two years later; the state was named Cheng, later Han, and is known as Cheng Han.

Han_Zhao.title: Liu Yuan founds Han Zhao
Han_Zhao.text: The Xiongnu noble Liu Yuan proclaimed himself King of Han and rose claiming the Han dynasty's legacy, opening the era of the Sixteen Kingdoms.

Emperor_Min_of_Jin.title: Fall of Chang'an; end of the Western Jin
Emperor_Min_of_Jin.text: The Han Zhao general Liu Yao took Chang'an; Emperor Min of Jin surrendered and the Western Jin came to an end.

Emperor_Yuan_of_Jin.title: Sima Rui becomes emperor; Eastern Jin founded
Emperor_Yuan_of_Jin.text: Backed by northern and southern gentry such as Wang Dao, Sima Rui, Prince of Langya, became emperor ("the Wang and the Sima share the realm"); the Eastern Jin held the south for over a century.

Later_Zhao.title: Shi Le founds Later Zhao
Later_Zhao.text: The Jie leader Shi Le broke away from Han Zhao, destroyed Former Zhao in 329 and united most of the north.

Former_Yan.title: Murong Huang founds Former Yan
Former_Yan.text: Murong Huang, chief of the Murong Xianbei, styled himself King of Yan; Former Yan later moved south into the Central Plains and stood alongside Eastern Jin and Former Qin.

Huan_Wen.title: Huan Wen destroys Cheng Han
Huan_Wen.text: The Eastern Jin general Huan Wen marched up the Yangtze and took Chengdu; Cheng Han fell and Ba-Shu returned to the Eastern Jin.

Former_Qin.title: Fu Jian founds Former Qin
Former_Qin.text: Fu Jian of the Di people entered Guanzhong and became king, then emperor the next year. Under Fu Jian (his nephew) and Wang Meng, Former Qin became the strongest state in the north.

Wang_Meng_(Former_Qin).title: Wang Meng destroys Former Yan
Wang_Meng_(Former_Qin).text: The Former Qin chancellor Wang Meng took Ye; Former Yan fell and all the land east of the passes passed to Former Qin.

Former_Liang.title: Former Qin destroys Former Liang
Former_Liang.text: Former Qin conquered Former Liang in the Hexi Corridor and destroyed the state of Dai in the same year, unifying the north.

Northern_Wei.title: Tuoba Gui founds Northern Wei
Northern_Wei.text: After Former Qin collapsed, the Xianbei Tuoba Gui restored his state as King of Dai and soon renamed it Wei, known as Northern Wei.

Battle_of_Canhe_Slope.title: Battle of Canhe Slope
Battle_of_Canhe_Slope.text: Northern Wei crushed the Later Yan army and buried the surrendered soldiers alive; dominance in the north began to shift to Northern Wei.

Later_Qin.title: Liu Yu's northern campaign destroys Later Qin
Later_Qin.text: The Eastern Jin strongman Liu Yu marched north and took Chang'an, ending Later Qin; but Guanzhong was soon taken by Helian Bobo.

Liu_Song_dynasty.title: Liu Yu replaces Jin and founds Song
Liu_Song_dynasty.text: Liu Yu deposed Emperor Gong of Jin and took the throne with the dynastic name Song, known as Liu Song; the Southern Dynasties began.

Northern_Liang.title: Northern Wei destroys Northern Liang and unifies the north
Northern_Liang.text: Emperor Taiwu of Northern Wei conquered Northern Liang, ending the Sixteen Kingdoms era of more than 130 years; the standoff with Liu Song in the south began the Northern and Southern Dynasties.

January_28_incident.title: January 28 Incident
January_28_incident.text: Japanese troops attacked Zhabei in Shanghai and the 19th Route Army fought back. The Shanghai Ceasefire Agreement was signed in May.

Manchukuo.title: Manchukuo (puppet state) founded
Manchukuo.text: Japan set up the puppet regime "Manchukuo" under Puyi, the last Qing emperor; the League of Nations refused to recognize it.

Defense_of_the_Great_Wall.title: Defense of the Great Wall
Defense_of_the_Great_Wall.text: Japanese troops took Chengde, capital of Rehe Province, and Chinese troops resisted them at the Great Wall passes for more than two months.

Tanggu_Truce.title: Tanggu Truce
Tanggu_Truce.text: The Sino-Japanese ceasefire made eastern Hebei a demilitarized zone, in effect accepting Japan's occupation of Manchuria and Rehe.

December_9th_Movement.title: December 9th Movement
December_9th_Movement.text: Students in Beiping demonstrated against "North China autonomy", calling for an end to civil war and united resistance to Japan.

Xi'an_Incident.title: Xi'an Incident
Xi'an_Incident.text: Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng detained Chiang Kai-shek, demanding an end to the civil war and alliance with the Communists against Japan. Its peaceful resolution led to the Second United Front.

Battle_of_Shanghai.title: Battle of Shanghai
Battle_of_Shanghai.text: Nearly a million troops on both sides fought for three months, thwarting Japan's hopes of a quick, decisive victory; Shanghai fell in November.

Battle_of_Pingxingguan.title: Battle of Pingxingguan
Battle_of_Pingxingguan.text: The Eighth Route Army's 115th Division ambushed a Japanese supply column, China's first victory since full-scale war began.

1938_Yellow_River_flood.title: Huayuankou dike breach
1938_Yellow_River_flood.text: The Nationalist Government broke the Yellow River dikes to slow the Japanese advance west; parts of Henan, Anhui and Jiangsu were flooded, hundreds of thousands died and millions were displaced.

Battle_of_Wuhan.title: Battle of Wuhan
Battle_of_Wuhan.text: The largest battle of the early war, lasting four and a half months. After Wuhan fell, the war entered a stalemate.

Bombing_of_Chongqing.title: Bombing of Chongqing
Bombing_of_Chongqing.text: From 1938 to 1943 Japan repeatedly bombed the wartime capital Chongqing indiscriminately, causing heavy civilian casualties.

Hundred_Regiments_Offensive.title: Hundred Regiments Offensive
Hundred_Regiments_Offensive.text: The Eighth Route Army launched a large sabotage offensive in North China, badly damaging Japanese lines of communication.

New_Fourth_Army_incident.title: New Fourth Army Incident
New_Fourth_Army_incident.text: Nationalist troops surrounded and destroyed the New Fourth Army headquarters as it moved north; Nationalist–Communist relations sharply worsened.

Battle_of_Hong_Kong.title: Battle of Hong Kong
Battle_of_Hong_Kong.text: Hours after the attack on Pearl Harbor, Japan attacked Hong Kong; the British surrendered on 25 December. China then formally declared war on Japan.

Operation_Ichi-Go.title: Operation Ichi-Go
Operation_Ichi-Go.text: Japan launched a campaign to open a continental supply corridor; Chinese armies collapsed and large parts of Henan, Hunan and Guangxi were lost.

Defense_of_Hengyang.title: Defense of Hengyang
Defense_of_Hengyang.text: Chinese defenders held the isolated city for 47 days, the longest city defense of the war.

Soviet_invasion_of_Manchuria.title: Soviet invasion of Manchuria
Soviet_invasion_of_Manchuria.text: The Soviet Union declared war on Japan; a million Soviet troops entered Manchuria and the Kwantung Army quickly collapsed.

Chongqing_Negotiations.title: Chongqing Negotiations
Chongqing_Negotiations.text: Mao Zedong went to Chongqing to negotiate with Chiang Kai-shek and signed the Double Tenth Agreement on 10 October, but the peace did not hold.

Chinese_Civil_War.title: Full-scale civil war breaks out
Chinese_Civil_War.text: Nationalist troops besieged the Central Plains Liberated Area, and the second Nationalist–Communist civil war broke out in full.

Battle_of_Yan'an.title: Hu Zongnan takes Yan'an
Battle_of_Yan'an.text: The CCP Central Committee deliberately left Yan'an and moved around northern Shaanxi; a year later the PLA retook Yan'an.

Battle_of_Menglianggu.title: Menglianggu Campaign
Battle_of_Menglianggu.text: The East China Field Army wiped out the Nationalist Reorganized 74th Division, defeating the focused offensive against Shandong.

Liaoshen_campaign.title: Liaoshen Campaign
Liaoshen_campaign.text: The Northeast Field Army took Jinzhou and besieged Changchun, and by 2 November held Shenyang; all of Manchuria changed hands.

Pingjin_campaign.title: Pingjin Campaign
Pingjin_campaign.text: The PLA took Tianjin; Fu Zuoyi, commander at Beiping, accepted peaceful reorganization, and the PLA entered Beiping on 31 January 1949.

Yangtze_River_Crossing_Campaign.title: Yangtze River Crossing Campaign
Yangtze_River_Crossing_Campaign.text: A million PLA troops crossed the Yangtze and took Nanjing, the Nationalist capital, on 23 April.

Battle_of_Guningtou.title: Battle of Guningtou
Battle_of_Guningtou.text: The PLA landing on Kinmen failed and the Nationalist Government held the island; the standoff across the Taiwan Strait gradually took shape.

Landing_Operation_on_Hainan_Island.title: Hainan Island Campaign
Landing_Operation_on_Hainan_Island.text: The PLA crossed the Qiongzhou Strait in wooden sailing junks and held all of Hainan Island by 1 May.

phases.tk_200: 200: Battle of Guandu; Cao Cao and Yuan Shao vie for the north
phases.tk_208: End of 208: Red Cliffs; Cao Cao holds the north
phases.tk_215: 215: Liu Bei holds Yi; Sun and Liu split Jing at the Xiang River
phases.tk_222: 222: After Yiling, the three kingdoms stand
phases.tk_266: 266: Sima Yan replaces Wei and founds the Jin
phases.tk_280: 280: Jin conquers Wu; the Three Kingdoms end
phases.wh_311: 311: Disaster of Yongjia; Han Zhao takes Luoyang
phases.wh_318: 318: Western Jin falls; Eastern Jin founded at Jiankang
phases.wh_330: 330: Later Zhao holds most of the north
phases.wh_395: 395: The north splits again after the Fei River
phases.wh_439: 439: Northern Wei unifies the north; North and South face off
phases.aj_1937: End of 1937: North China, Nanjing, Shanghai and Hangzhou fall
phases.aj_1938: October 1938: Wuhan and Guangzhou fall; stalemate begins
phases.aj_1941: End of 1941: Pacific War begins; Japan enters Indochina
phases.aj_1944: End of 1944: Japanese occupation at its peak after Ichi-Go
phases.cw_1946: June 1946: Full-scale civil war breaks out
phases.cw_1947: End of 1947: PLA goes on the strategic offensive
phases.cw_1948: November 1948: Liaoshen Campaign ends; all of Manchuria changes hands
phases.cw_1949a: January 1949: Huaihai and Pingjin campaigns end
phases.cw_1949b: 1 October 1949: People's Republic of China founded
phases.cw_1950: May 1950: Hainan Island Campaign; Nationalist Government withdraws to Taiwan
